rationale: I own these shares, bought a week ago at $251.845 and now marked down about 11%. A price decline with no change in the business is not a sell trigger. It is the market offering me the same company for less. The numbers I can see are good: five-year average ROE of 26.9%, debt-to-equity of 0.32, and owner earnings averaging about $9.26 billion against a $134 billion market cap. But I would not lean on the 49.86% margin of safety. It rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, which is a generous setup, and the snapshot says nothing about ten years of earnings, CEO tenure or moat metrics. So I keep what I have, add nothing until I can confirm those gaps, and watch whether technology change erodes the consulting franchise.

rationale: I don't own NEU, and the numbers in front of me are attractive: a 30.6% five-year average ROE, debt-to-equity of 0.43, a $6.58 billion market cap and a 44.9% margin of safety against the model's intrinsic value. But I'm not going to buy on the fields that happen to be present. The snapshot doesn't show ten years of earnings, management tenure or capital allocation history, and I can't test the long-term threat to the franchise from changing demand for the products behind these additives. The DCF also leans on 8% growth (the trailing 13.9% CAGR was capped) and a 5% discount rate, which makes it sensitive, so I treat that margin of safety with suspicion until I've checked the rest. A good business at a cheap-looking price isn't enough; I'll wait until I can confirm the earnings record and the durability of the moat. Until then, I sit on my hands.

rationale: I understand this business: it sells other people's consumer electronics and appliances out of big boxes and online. The price looks fair, at $97.14 against a computed value of $117.52, and the numbers clear the screen on size, leverage and a 17% discount. But I can't find a moat. The products are made by someone else, shoppers can compare prices with a phone, and the brand gives no pricing power I can see. A business like that has to earn its return again every year, and the high ROE of 48% looks to me more like a small equity base than a franchise. A cheap price on a retailer with no durable advantage is the cigar-butt thinking I left behind after See's. I'll pass and wait for a better pitch.

rationale: The screen numbers look good: a 45% margin of safety, a 22% five-year average ROE and debt-to-equity of 0.43. But I don't own this name, and a cheap price alone doesn't get me to buy. The snapshot gives me only a ticker, with no business description, no moat evidence and no earnings history. I can't write the two-paragraph explanation with the confidence I demand, and I can't confirm a moat that will last ten years. Services businesses that sell labor and process work are exposed to technological change that could make their moat something that has to be rebuilt every year, and I have always said a moat that must be continuously rebuilt is no moat at all. A low price on a business I can't predict is exactly the trap I try to avoid. I'll pass and wait for a pitch squarely in my sweet spot.

exit_trigger: ROE falls below 15% in a sustained way, showing the franchise economics are gone; Evidence of brand erosion: forced discounting, falling premium pricing, or loss of customer loyalty; Operating cash flow turns negative or management is shown to be dishonest or to destroy value through acquisitions; Price rises above 1.5x a defensible intrinsic value and stays there; A far better opportunity at much higher conviction
rationale: We own ten shares, bought at $128.38 and now marked at $103.61, down 19.3% after 108 days, and the question is whether to keep them. The numbers in front of me are the kind I like: a 34.6% average ROE over five years, a debt-to-equity of 0.0, and owner earnings of about $1.32 billion against a market cap of about $10.9 billion. The model says $363 a share, but that rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on a 71% margin of safety from a spreadsheet, so I haircut it heavily. My real worry is that this is a brand tied to apparel fashion, and fashion is a moat that must be rebuilt each season, which is no moat at all if it fails. A lower price does not make me sell, and nothing in this snapshot shows the moat has eroded, so I keep what we own, I do not add until I can confirm ten years of earnings and pricing power, and I stay ready to sell if the brand's economics crack.

exit_trigger: Franchise test fails: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years; Reported negative annual operating cash flow in any of the newest five fiscal years; Evidence of pricing power eroding as AI-based competitors take customers; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value on a persistent basis
rationale: I don't own Adobe, and the numbers in front of me are the kind that make an old man sit up: a 5-year average ROE of 40.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.41, and a price of $221.40 against a computed value of $467.50. But I'd be careful with that margin of safety. It rests on a 5% discount rate and 8% growth, and a small change in those inputs moves it a lot. The bigger question is whether a business built on creative software will still have its pricing power ten years out, now that machines can make images and documents on their own. I can't answer that with the confidence I'd want, and the snapshot doesn't give me the ten-year earnings record or the management history to lean on. So I keep it on the list and wait. If I can't tell where the moat stands in ten years, I'd rather pass than guess.

exit_trigger: 5-year ROE falls so that ROE ≥ 15% fails in more than 20% of fiscal years; Negative annual operating cash flow reported; Price rises above 1.5x owner-earnings intrinsic value; Manufacturer relationships or service profit streams erode materially; Evidence of management dishonesty or value-destroying acquisitions
rationale: I own six shares of Penske Automotive at a basis of $216.77, and they now trade at $212.60, down about 1.9% — noise, not a reason to act. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.40, and a margin of safety of 18.2% against an owner-earnings value of $260 per share. That clears my 15% threshold, but it rests on zero assumed growth at a 5% discount rate, and the snapshot gives me nothing on earnings consistency, ten-year history, or CEO tenure, so I cannot say every criterion is met. Auto retail is a decent business, not a See's Candies; the moat is scale and service, and I hold it with modest conviction. I keep what I own, add only if the price falls or I learn more, and I sell only if the franchise erodes.

exit_trigger: 5-year average ROE falls so that ROE >= 15% holds in fewer than 80% of fiscal years; Negative annual operating cash flow, signaling management or execution failure; Price above 1.5x owner-earnings intrinsic value on a persistent basis; Evidence of dishonest or value-destroying capital allocation, such as large acquisitions at peak prices; Structural loss of incumbency on core programs
rationale: I own General Dynamics, so the question is whether to keep it, and I keep it. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 17.2% and debt-to-equity of 0.30, both inside my thresholds, and the owner-earnings DCF gives about $417 a share against a $344.62 price, a 17.4% margin of safety. That clears my 15% bar, though not by a wide margin, and the valuation leans on an 8% growth rate that was capped from a trailing 8.7%. The moat is the kind of position that comes from being an incumbent supplier of submarines and other defense platforms to one dominant customer, a franchise that is hard to dislodge, but I cannot verify the backlog, contract structure or management record from this snapshot. We are down 2.43% after 26 days, which tells me nothing; a price decline with the franchise intact is no reason to sell. I would hold the one share and not add until I could check the data I am missing.
